raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable electrical therapy for patients with persistent heart failure (HF) symptoms despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), particularly those with reduced or mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and a QRS duration that does not support cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) [1,2]. This therapeutic niche is clinically important because CRT improves outcomes in appropriately selected patients with electrical dyssynchrony [3,4], yet many symptomatic patients have narrow QRS complexes or do not respond to CRT. CCM differs fundamentally from pacing: it delivers relatively high-voltage, biphasic, non-excitatory impulses to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, thereby avoiding a new propagated depolarization while modulating myocardial contractile biology [5].

Early experimental and translational work established biological plausibility. Non-excitatory electrical signals increased contractility in isolated and in-vivo preparations [5,6], and acute human studies showed improved left ventricular systolic performance in ischemic and idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy [7]. Initial chronic human experience suggested feasibility, acceptable safety, and improvements in functional status and quality-of-life metrics [8]. Importantly, the acute inotropic effect appears distinct from catecholamine-like pharmacologic inotropy: in patients and animal models, CCM enhanced ventricular performance without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption [9]. This observation is central to its appeal in HF, where conventional chronic positive inotropes have historically raised safety concerns.

The clinical evidence base has evolved through sham-controlled crossover trials, randomized studies, subgroup analyses, and registries. The FIX-HF-4 trial showed improvements in peak oxygen consumption and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire scores, although placebo effects were notable [10]. The FIX-HF-5 program was designed to assess safety and efficacy in advanced systolic HF [11]. Molecular biopsy data from CCM-treated patients showed partial reversal of fetal-gene expression and normalization of calcium-handling genes, including SERCA2a-related pathways, supporting a disease-modifying mechanistic signal rather than a purely hemodynamic effect [12]. Mechanistic studies have also implicated altered action potential duration, beta-adrenergic signaling, calcium cycling, phosphorylation pathways, and reverse remodeling [13].

The pivotal FIX-HF-5 experience was nuanced: the overall trial had mixed efficacy results, but prespecified and subsequent analyses suggested greater benefit among patients with LVEF approximately 25–45%, NYHA class III symptoms, and QRS <130 ms [14]. FIX-HF-5C then prospectively tested this enriched population and demonstrated improvements in exercise tolerance, quality of life, and functional class, with acceptable device-related safety [15]. Contemporary mechanistic reviews emphasize that the strongest signal lies in patients with symptomatic HF, LVEF 25–45%, narrow QRS, and no standard CRT indication [16].

Evidence synthesis broadly supports symptomatic and functional benefit. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found improvements in quality of life and exercise capacity without a clear mortality signal [17]. An individual-patient-data meta-analysis confirmed favorable effects on peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, and HF-related quality of life, with larger responses in patients with LVEF ≥35% [18]. Longer-term real-world studies suggest reductions in HF hospitalization and potentially favorable survival compared with risk-model predictions, although these findings remain susceptible to confounding because they are observational [19-21]. The 2-lead Optimizer Smart system simplified implantation by eliminating the atrial lead and showed comparable signal delivery and clinical performance in FIX-HF-5C2 [22]. Practical implantation and programming considerations resemble transvenous rhythm-device practice but require attention to septal lead positioning, sensing windows, and avoidance of stimulation outside refractoriness [23,24].

Patient selection is therefore pivotal. Candidates are generally patients with persistent NYHA class III symptoms despite GDMT, LVEF 25–45%, sinus rhythm or manageable atrial rhythm depending on device generation and local labeling, QRS duration not meeting CRT criteria, and reasonable expectation of adherence to device follow-up and charging. CCM is not a substitute for GDMT, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy when indicated, CRT in eligible patients, valve intervention, revascularization, or advanced HF therapies. Conversely, it may be useful when symptoms and impaired functional capacity persist after these options have been optimized.

Emerging work is expanding the conceptual boundaries of CCM. Preclinical and early clinical data suggest effects on diastolic function and myocardial stiffness pathways, raising interest in HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [25]. A pilot CCM-HFpEF study reported improved Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores and acceptable short-term safety, but definitive randomized data are lacking [26]. Economic modeling suggests potential cost-effectiveness in selected patients with narrow QRS if clinical benefits persist beyond trial follow-up [27]. Recent reviews appropriately frame CCM as a complementary device therapy with promising symptom and hospitalization signals, but not yet a therapy with proven mortality reduction [28-30]. Future priorities include adequately powered sham-controlled trials, integration with contemporary quadruple GDMT, clearer biomarkers of response, evaluation in atrial fibrillation and HFpEF, and long-term comparative effectiveness against other device-based and advanced HF strategies.
